theory.intro: The **distribution** of a dataset is the way its values are spread out. One half of describing a distribution's shape is its **modality** — how many **peaks** the data has. A **peak** is a value, or a group of neighbouring values, whose frequency is higher than the frequencies on either side of it, so modality can be read straight off a column graph, a dot plot, a frequency table or a smooth curve.
facts: **Uniform**: every value occurs equally often, so the display is flat and there is **no peak**. A uniform dataset has **no mode**.
**Bimodal**: the data has **two** peaks, separated by lower frequencies.
**Multimodal**: the data has **three or more** peaks.
Peaks do **not** have to be the same height. Two clear peaks of very different heights still make a distribution bimodal.
Two tallest columns that sit **side by side** form a single peak, not two — separate peaks must have a dip between them.

foundation.solution_text:
Every column has the same height, so no hour stands out and there is no peak.
Uniform, and there is no mode.

$6$am, $8$am and $10$am are each taller than the columns on either side of them, so there are three peaks.
Multimodal.

The stacks build up to a single tallest stack at $3$ and then get shorter, so there is one peak.
Unimodal.

The tallest stacks are at $2$ and at $7$, and the stacks between them are much shorter, so there are two peaks.
Bimodal.

foundation.question_text:
The frequency table shows the number of songs on each of $27$ playlists.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{Songs per playlist} & \text{Frequency} \\ \hline 10\text{--}14 & 2 \\ \hline 15\text{--}19 & 5 \\ \hline 20\text{--}24 & 11 \\ \hline 25\text{--}29 & 6 \\ \hline 30\text{--}34 & 3 \\ \hline \end{array}$
Describe the modality of this distribution.
foundation.solution_text:
The frequencies rise $2, 5, 11$ and then fall $6, 3$, so there is one peak, at $20\text{--}24$ songs.
Unimodal.

A column is a peak when it is taller than the columns on either side of it.
$7$am is taller than $6$am and $8$am, and $10$am is taller than $9$am and $11$am.
$2$ peaks.

The curve shows the distribution of the number of songs on a large collection of playlists. Describe the modality of this distribution.
foundation.solution_text:
The curve rises to a single high point and then falls away, so there is one peak.
Unimodal.

development.solution_text:
$6$am is taller than the columns on either side of it, and so is $10$am, so there are two peaks with a dip between them.
The peaks do not need to be the same height.
Bimodal.

Every value has a stack of $4$ dots, so the dot plot is flat and no value stands out.
Uniform, and there is no mode.

The stacks at $1$, $4$ and $7$ are each taller than the stacks on either side of them, so there are three peaks.
Multimodal.

development.question_text:
The frequency table shows the number of buses arriving each hour, recorded over $29$ hours.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{Buses per hour} & \text{Frequency} \\ \hline 0\text{--}2 & 3 \\ \hline 3\text{--}5 & 9 \\ \hline 6\text{--}8 & 4 \\ \hline 9\text{--}11 & 2 \\ \hline 12\text{--}14 & 8 \\ \hline 15\text{--}17 & 3 \\ \hline \end{array}$
Describe the modality of this distribution.
development.solution_text:
The frequencies rise to $9$ at $3\text{--}5$, fall to $2$ at $9\text{--}11$, then rise again to $8$ at $12\text{--}14$.
Two peaks separated by a dip.
Bimodal.

development.solution_text:
$A$ is flat, so it is uniform. $C$ rises to one tall column and falls away, so it is unimodal.
$B$ has two tall columns separated by a dip, so it has two peaks.
Display $B$.

mastery.question_text:
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.85]\draw[->] (0,0)--(0,4.6);\draw[->] (0,0)--(8.2,0);\draw[thick] plot[smooth,tension=0.6] coordinates {(0.2,0.1)(0.9,1.2)(1.6,3.2)(2.3,1.1)(3,0.7)(3.7,2)(4.4,0.8)(5.1,0.6)(5.8,2.6)(6.5,1)(7.2,0.2)};\node[rotate=90,font=\scriptsize] at (-1.1,1.6) {Number of trains};\node[below,font=\scriptsize] at (3.6,-1.0) {Time of day};\node[font=\small] at (3.6,4.3) {Trains across a day};\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
The curve shows the distribution of the number of trains arriving across a day. Describe the modality of this distribution, and explain why the different heights of the high points do not change your answer.
mastery.solution_text:
The curve rises and falls three times, so there are three peaks.
Modality counts how many peaks there are, not how tall they are, so three high points of different heights still give three peaks.
Multimodal.
